advances: Proves the locked weak bound for every actual convex body with one integer coordinate that is invariant under reversal of that coordinate, for every continuous dimension, with the single absolute constant \(c_0=1/(3e)\). The selected point lies in the actual origin fiber. The argument compares horizontal lattice counts to a continuous Minkowski enlargement and requires no hypothesis on the shapes or centroid rank of the integer fibers.
author: research-agent
external_sources: Branko Grünbaum, “Partitions of mass-distributions and of convex bodies by hyperplanes,” Pacific Journal of Mathematics 10 (1960), 1257–1261, [primary publisher PDF](https://msp.org/pjm/1960/10-4/pjm-v10-n4-p18-p.pdf). Section 3, printed page 1259, proves the following centroid form of Theorem 2: if \(K\subset\mathbb R^q\) is a convex body with volume centroid \(g_K\), then every closed halfspace \(H\) containing \(g_K\) satisfies \(\operatorname{vol}_q(K\cap H)\ge(q/(q+1))^q\operatorname{vol}_q(K)\). Here \(K=\widetilde C\), \(q=d+1\), and \(g_K=(0,m)\); compactness, convexity, full dimensionality, and the centroid identity were proved above. For \(\beta\ne0\), the halfspace \(H=\mathbb R\times E_\beta\) contains this centroid, so this theorem applies exactly to (4). No other external theorem is used.
proof:
The projection \(D\) is nonempty, compact, and convex. If \(y\in D\), choose \(x\) with \((x,y)\in C\). Base reversal also puts \((-x,y)\) in \(C\), so their midpoint \((0,y)\) lies in \(C\). This proves \(D\subseteq C_0\); the reverse inclusion follows from the definition of \(D\). Thus \(D=C_0\).

The horizontal section at each \(y\in D\) is a nonempty compact convex subset of \(\mathbb R\), invariant under sign reversal. Consequently it is exactly \([-\rho(y),\rho(y)]\), including the singleton case \(\rho(y)=0\). The maximum defining \(\rho\) exists and is nonnegative. Compactness of \(C\) bounds \(\rho\). It also makes \(\rho\) upper semicontinuous on \(D\): for any sequence \(y_j\to y\) in \(D\), a subsequence realizing the limsup of \(\rho(y_j)\) has its points \((\rho(y_j),y_j)\) converge to a point of the closed set \(C\), whose first coordinate is at most \(\rho(y)\). Hence \(\rho\), \(N\), and \(v\) are measurable.

The horizontal lattice count is exactly \(N(y)\). Endpoints of the section are included, so this formula also holds when \(\rho(y)\) is an integer. For \(k=\lfloor\rho(y)\rfloor\ge0\),

\[
N(y)=2k+1\le 2\rho(y)+1=v(y)<2k+3\le3(2k+1)=3N(y).
\tag{1}
\]

Outside \(D\), both sides are zero, so \(N\le v\le3N\) holds everywhere. There are only finitely many integers \(z\) with \(C_z\ne\varnothing\), by boundedness of \(C\). Applying Fubini to their indicator functions gives, for every measurable \(E\subseteq\mathbb R^d\),

\[
\mathcal H_d\bigl(S\cap(\mathbb R\times E)\bigr)
=\sum_{z\in\mathbb Z}\operatorname{vol}_d(C_z\cap E)
=\int_E N(y)\,dy.
\tag{2}
\]

In particular, \(W=\int N\). Zero-volume integer fibers contribute zero in this formula. Since \(C\) is full-dimensional, it contains an open Euclidean ball, whose projection contains an open \(d\)-dimensional ball in \(D\). Thus \(\operatorname{vol}_d(D)>0\). Because \(N\ge1\) on \(D\), it follows that \(W\ge\operatorname{vol}_d(D)>0\). This also proves \(S\ne\varnothing\) directly. The zero-volume case in the locked problem, if considered separately, needs only its nonempty-set hypothesis to choose a point with a nonnegative depth and a zero right-hand side.

The Minkowski sum \(\widetilde C\) is compact and convex: it is the continuous image of the compact product \(C\times[-1/2,1/2]\) under addition, and convex combinations of sums are sums of the corresponding convex combinations. It contains \(C\), so it is full-dimensional. Adding the segment changes no \(y\)-coordinate. Its horizontal section at \(y\in D\) is therefore exactly \([-\rho(y)-1/2,\rho(y)+1/2]\), of length \(v(y)\), and its horizontal sections outside \(D\) are empty. Fubini proves the asserted marginal and total-volume identities. Integrating (1) yields

\[
W\le\widetilde W\le3W.
\tag{3}
\]

For completeness, the marginal is log-concave by an elementary section argument. For \(y_0,y_1\in D\) and \(t\in[0,1]\), convexity applied to \((\rho(y_0),y_0)\) and \((\rho(y_1),y_1)\) gives \(\rho(ty_0+(1-t)y_1)\ge t\rho(y_0)+(1-t)\rho(y_1)\). Thus \(v\) is positive and concave on \(D\). The weighted arithmetic-geometric mean inequality gives \(v(ty_0+(1-t)y_1)\ge v(y_0)^t v(y_1)^{1-t}\). For \(0<t<1\), if either endpoint is outside \(D\), the right-hand side of the log-concavity inequality for the zero extension is zero. The endpoint cases \(t=0,1\) are immediate. Hence the zero extension, and its probability normalization \(v/\widetilde W\), are log-concave. The centroid-cap estimate below uses the actual convex body \(\widetilde C\) directly, so it needs no separate theorem about log-concave densities.

Base reversal preserves \(\widetilde C\) and ordinary volume, and therefore the first coordinate of its volume centroid is zero. Fubini and the marginal identity show that its other coordinates equal the stated \(m\). The integrals exist because the support is compact and \(\widetilde W>0\).

The point \(m\) belongs to \(D\). To prove this without any assertion about fiber centroids, suppose \(m\notin D\), and let \(k\in D\) be a nearest point. With \(\delta=m-k\ne0\), minimizing squared distance along the segment from \(k\) to any \(y\in D\) gives \(\delta\cdot(y-k)\le0\). Integrating against the probability density \(v/\widetilde W\) gives \(\delta\cdot(m-k)\le0\), contradicting \(\|\delta\|_2^2>0\). As \(D=C_0\), the point \((0,m)\) is an actual member of \(S\), selected before any halfspace.

Fix \(\beta\in\mathbb R^d\), and put \(E_\beta=\{y:\beta\cdot(y-m)\ge0\}\). If \(\beta\ne0\), the closed ambient halfspace \(\mathbb R\times E_\beta\) contains the centroid \((0,m)\) of the convex body \(\widetilde C\). Grünbaum's centroid halfspace inequality, in dimension \(d+1\), gives

\[
\int_{E_\beta}v(y)\,dy
=\operatorname{vol}_{d+1}\bigl(\widetilde C\cap(\mathbb R\times E_\beta)\bigr)
\ge\gamma_{d+1}\widetilde W.
\tag{4}
\]

If \(\beta=0\), then \(E_\beta=\mathbb R^d\), so (4) still holds, since \(\gamma_{d+1}\le1\). From (1), (3), and (4), with the original lattice count rather than a reweighted law, we obtain

\[
\int_{E_\beta}N(y)\,dy
\ge\frac13\int_{E_\beta}v(y)\,dy
\ge\frac{\gamma_{d+1}}3\widetilde W
\ge\frac{\gamma_{d+1}}3W.
\tag{5}
\]

Now fix arbitrary \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\) and \(\beta\in\mathbb R^d\). For \(z\in\mathbb Z\) and \(y\in C_z\), the pointwise inequality

\[
\mathbf1_{\{\alpha z+\beta\cdot(y-m)\ge0\}}
+\mathbf1_{\{-\alpha z+\beta\cdot(y-m)\ge0\}}
\ge\mathbf1_{\{\beta\cdot(y-m)\ge0\}}
\tag{6}
\]

holds: if the last scalar is nonnegative, at least one of the first two scalars is nonnegative. Define \(H_{\alpha,\beta}=\{(x,y):\alpha x+\beta\cdot(y-m)\ge0\}\). Base reversal gives \(C_{-z}=C_z\). Reindexing the original finite mixed-volume sum by \(z\mapsto-z\) therefore shows \(\mathcal H_d(S\cap H_{\alpha,\beta})=\mathcal H_d(S\cap H_{-\alpha,\beta})\). Integrating (6) over every original integer fiber, and using (2) and (5), yields

\[
2\mathcal H_d(S\cap H_{\alpha,\beta})
\ge\sum_{z\in\mathbb Z}\operatorname{vol}_d(C_z\cap E_\beta)
=\int_{E_\beta}N(y)\,dy
\ge\frac{\gamma_{d+1}}3W.
\tag{7}
\]

This includes \(\alpha=0\), \(\beta=0\), and zero-volume fibers. Every proper closed halfspace containing \((0,m)\) can be written \(H=\{(x,y):\alpha x+\beta\cdot y\ge a\}\), with \((\alpha,\beta)\ne0\) and \(a\le\beta\cdot m\). It contains \(H_{\alpha,\beta}\). Equation (7) thus bounds its original mixed-integer volume below by \(\gamma_{d+1}W/6\). If the whole space is allowed as a halfspace, its volume is \(W\) and it satisfies the same bound. Taking the infimum in the locked definition gives the asserted depth estimate.

Finally, \(\log(1+t)=\int_0^t(1+s)^{-1}\,ds<t\) for \(t>0\). Therefore \(\log\gamma_{d+1}=-(d+1)\log(1+1/(d+1))>-1\), so \(\gamma_{d+1}>1/e\). This proves the claimed bound with the fixed absolute constant \(c_0=1/(3e)\), which lies strictly between zero and \(1/e\).
statement:
Let \(d\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\), let \(C\subset\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d\) be a convex body invariant under \((x,y)\mapsto(-x,y)\), and let \(S=C\cap(\mathbb Z\times\mathbb R^d)\ne\varnothing\). Use the locked mixed-integer volume and halfspace depth. For \(z\in\mathbb Z\), put \(C_z=\{y:(z,y)\in C\}\), \(w_z=\operatorname{vol}_d(C_z)\), \(D_+=\{z:w_z>0\}\), and \(W=\sum_{z\in D_+}w_z=\mathcal H_d(S)\). These recurring objects have their canonical actual-fiber meanings.

Put \(D=\{y:\exists x\ (x,y)\in C\}\). For \(y\in D\), let \(\rho(y)=\max\{x:(x,y)\in C\}\), and define \(N(y)=2\lfloor\rho(y)\rfloor+1\) and \(v(y)=2\rho(y)+1\); set both \(N\) and \(v\) equal to zero outside \(D\). The registered subgoal's horizontal radius \(r(y)\) and scalar marginal \(V(y)\) are denoted \(\rho(y)\) and \(v(y)\), respectively, to distinguish them from recurring centroid-rank and profile notation.

The body \(\widetilde C=C+([-1/2,1/2]\times\{0_d\})\) has \(y\)-marginal \(v\). Define \(\widetilde W=\operatorname{vol}_{d+1}(\widetilde C)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}v(y)\,dy\), \(m=\widetilde W^{-1}\int_{\mathbb R^d}y\,v(y)\,dy\), and \(\gamma_{d+1}=((d+1)/(d+2))^{d+1}\). Then \(m\in D=C_0\), the centroid of \(\widetilde C\) is \((0,m)\), and this one fixed actual point \(\mathbf y^\star=(0,m)\in S\) satisfies

\[
h_S(\mathbf y^\star)\ge\frac{\gamma_{d+1}}6\,W
\ge\frac1{6e}\,W
=\frac{1/(3e)}{2^1}\,\mathcal H_d(S).
\]

In particular, this is the locked bound with \(c_0=1/(3e)\in(0,1/e)\) on the stated entire subclass, independently of \(d\) and \(C\). If the locked zero-volume branch occurs, its requested inequality is automatic for any point of \(S\); under the full-dimensional convex-body and base-reversal hypotheses here, in fact \(W>0\).
